({{IPAc-en|w|aɪ|s}}, {{IPAc-en|w|aɪ|z}}), doing business as '''Weis''' and stylized as '''weis''', is an American [[Grocery store|food retailer]] headquartered in [[Sunbury, Pennsylvania]]."[http://www.weismarkets.com/about-weis/contact-us/ Contact Us]." ([https://web.archive.org/web/20120505152641/http://www.weismarkets.com/about-weis/contact-us/ Archive]) Weis Markets. Retrieved on August 26, 2016. "1000 South Second Street PO Box 471 Sunbury, Pennsylvania 17801" It currently operates 200 stores with over 23,000 employees in [[Pennsylvania]], [[Maryland]], [[New York (state)|New York]], [[New Jersey]], [[West Virginia]], [[Virginia]], and [[Delaware]]. ==History== ===20th century=== [[File:WeisMarkets footprint.png|thumb|A map of Weis stores as of 2011]] [[File:Weis Markets store in Conshohocken PA.jpeg|thumb|Weis Markets location in [[Conshohocken, Pennsylvania]], formerly a [[Genuardi's]]]] Weis Markets was founded as Weis Pure Foods in 1912 in [[Sunbury, Pennsylvania]], by two brothers, Harry and Sigmund Weis. Their store has been noted as "revolutionary" since it did not operate on credit; sales were only for cash. At the time, similar stores operated on credit, allowing customers to build a tab that would be paid periodically. Cash sales were a sign of a growing working class earning steady paychecks, and they also helped lower prices by up to 25%. Three years later, in 1915, a second Weis store opened in [[Harrisburg, Pennsylvania]]. The Weis brothers expanded the chain rapidly, opening dozens of small, in-town grocery stores throughout central [[Pennsylvania]], ultimately peaking at 115 stores in 15 central Pennsylvania counties in 1933. As the supermarket industry shifted to larger, self-service stores, Weis adapted the format of its stores. The company closed several corner grocery stores in Harrisburg in 1938, replacing them with their first self-service, consolidated supermarket. In newspaper ads during the 1940s, Weis referred to its stores first as Weis Super Markets,Advertisement, Harrisburg Telegraph, 6 March 1941 then Weis Self-Service Markets,Advertisement, Harrisburg Telegraph, 22 August 1946 and finally Weis Markets.Advertisement, The Express (Lock Haven, Pennsylvania), 9 December 1949 Over the next two decades, the company continued with this strategy, and it had consolidated all of its corner grocery stores into supermarkets, with 35 stores by 1955. In the 1950s and 1960s, Weis expanded its reach, first to [[York, Pennsylvania|York]] and then [[Lancaster, Pennsylvania|Lancaster]] by 1960. Weis expanded to [[Maryland]] in July 1967, opening its first non-Pennsylvania store in [[Hagerstown, Maryland|Hagerstown]],"Weis Markets Sales, Earnings Show Increases," The News (Frederick, Maryland), 18 Jul 1967 followed by a store in [[Frederick, Maryland|Frederick]] in August"Weis Markets Opens 2d Store in Maryland," Pottstown Mercury, 23 Aug 1967. Its first store in the [[Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania|Wilkes-Barre]] area opened in 1967."To Build Market," The News (Frederick, Maryland), 24 Oct 1967) In November 1967, the company purchased the five-store Albany Public Markets chain based in [[Albany, New York]], in an all-cash transaction. It operated Albany Public Markets as a subsidiary, keeping the company's management team intact."Weis Buys N.Y. Chain," The Express (Lock Haven, Pennsylvania), 8 Nov 1967) Weis closed its Albany Public Markets chain in October 1986, leasing the nine stores to [[Grand Union (supermarket)|Grand Union]].{{cite web|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1917&dat=19861009&id=kAwhAAAAIBAJ&sjid=U3IFAAAAIBAJ&pg=4334,2448674&hl=en|title=Schenectady Gazette - Google News Archive Search|website=news.google.com|access-date=24 October 2017}} Weis also expanded to [[Western Pennsylvania]], opening stores as far west as [[Altoona, Pennsylvania|Altoona]], [[Everett, Pennsylvania|Everett]], and [[Philipsburg, Centre County, Pennsylvania|Philipsburg]], and expanded throughout [[Northeastern Pennsylvania]]. The company purchased two regional chains in the [[Pocono Mountains|Poconos]] and [[Lehigh Valley]] region: Mr. Z's, a 14-store chain of IGA supermarkets, in 1992,"Weis Markets to Buy IGA Stores," Standard-Speaker (Hazleton, Pennsylvania), 28 November 1992 and King's, a six-store chain based in [[Hamburg, Pennsylvania|Hamburg]], in 1994."Weis Markets Inc. to Buy King's Supermarkets," Gettysburg Times, 29 June 1994{{cite web|url=https://www.mcall.com/1994/06/26/weis-buys-kings-six-markets/|title=Weis Buys King's Six Markets|date=26 June 1994 |access-date=24 October 2017}} Mr. Z's and King's were operated under separate banners for years before all stores were re-branded as Weis. The westernmost extent of Weis's expansion is along old route 220 with the two stores in Altoona, one on 7th street and one in Park Hills. Weis's expansion into the [[Baltimore]], market was successful, but expansions into the [[Washington, D.C.]] market were less successful. Weis opened stores in [[Northern Virginia]] before retreating from that market, first closing most of its stores in [[Montgomery County, Maryland]], and finally closing all stores in [[Virginia]]. Weis also expanded into [[North Jersey]], beginning with a store opened in [[Newton, New Jersey|Newton]] in 1992. ===21st century=== [[File:A_Weis_Markets_supermarket_in_Solomons,_Maryland_06.jpg|thumb|The produce section of a Weis Markets location]] In 2000, another store opened in [[Flanders, New Jersey|Flanders]]; it closed in 2002, two years after its opening. Weis returned to Flanders in 2014, in a former [[A&P]] store adjacent to the location of its first Flanders store.{{cite web|url=http://newjerseyhills.com/mt_olive_chronicle/news/weis-market-work-to-begin-in-mount-olive/article_83a8b5ee-0437-11e3-bde1-001a4bcf887a.html|title=Weis market work to begin in Mount Olive|date=16 August 2013 |access-date=24 October 2017}} In 2009, Weis expanded into the [[Southern Tier]] of New York with the acquisition of the 11-store [[Giant Markets]] chain.{{cite web|url=http://www.dailyitem.com/news/weis-markets-buys-stores/article_c05d6245-75e6-5693-b489-5779ad3619bc.html?$G1Ref|title=Weis Markets buys 11 stores |first=Wayne|last=Laepple|website=www.dailyitem.com|date=25 August 2009 |access-date=25 August 2009}} Weis closed one former Giant Market in [[Binghamton, New York|Binghamton]] in 2012, along with two others in 2014. Eight former Giant Markets continue to operate.{{cite web|url=http://wnbf.com/closing-time-for-two-broome-weis-markets-stores/?$G1Ref|title= Closing Time For Two Broome Weis Markets Stores|first=Bob|last=Joseph|website=www.wnbf.com|date= 17 July 2014|access-date=17 July 2014}} In 2012, eastern expansion continued as Weis acquired three former [[Genuardi's]] stores from [[Safeway Inc.|Safeway]], in the [[Philadelphia]] suburbs of [[Conshohocken, Pennsylvania|Conshohocken]], [[Doylestown, Pennsylvania|Doylestown]] and [[Norristown, Pennsylvania|Norristown]], on June 16. A former [[Superfresh]] store in [[Towson, Maryland]], opened as a Weis in 2012. Weis entered [[central New Jersey]] with the purchase of a former [[Pathmark]] store in [[Hillsborough Township, New Jersey|Hillsborough]] in August 2013. In November 2013, Weis opened its closest store to [[Philadelphia]] following its acquisition of a former Pathmark store in [[Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania]]. In July 2015, Weis purchased the location and assets of Nell's Shur-fine Market from C&S Wholesale Grocers in [[Penn Township, York County, Pennsylvania]] and followed that up in October 2016 with the purchase of a second Nell's location in [[East Berlin, Pennsylvania]].{{cite news|last=Jurgensen|first=Davin|title=Weis Markets purchasing Nell's Shur-fine Market|work=York Daily Record|date=July 29, 2015|url=http://www.ydr.com/story/money/2015/07/29/weis-markets-purchasing-nells-shur-fine-market/32443421/|access-date=October 19, 2016}}{{cite news|last=Sholtis|first=Brett|title=Weis to buy Nell's Family Market in East Berlin|work=York Daily Record|date=October 19, 2015|url=http://www.ydr.com/story/news/2016/10/06/weis-buy-nells-family-market-east-berlin/91602654/|access-date=October 19, 2016}} Robert F. Weis, the son of Harry Weis, died in October 2015 at the age of 96. A philanthropist, Weis donated millions of dollars to charities, food banks, and other organizations in Sunbury, the Central Susquehanna Valley, and elsewhere. A strong supporter of Israel, he sponsored a flight of Jewish survivors of the [[Chernobyl disaster]] to make [[aliyah]], and served as treasurer of the Sunbury chapter of the [[United Jewish Appeal]]. Weis was a member of Sunbury's Congregation Beth El and he helped found the Department of Judaic Studies at Yale University.{{cite web|url=https://www.winsightgrocerybusiness.com/weis-markets-founder-robert-f-weis-dies |title=Weis Markets Founder Robert F. Weis Dies |publisher=Winsight Grocery Business |accessdate=2023-04-06}} In May 2016, Weis Markets announced the purchase of five stores from [[Mars (supermarket)|Mars]] in [[Baltimore County, Maryland]], after that chain announced it was closing all its stores.{{cite news|last=Mirabella|first=Lorraine|title=Mars Super Markets closed all stores on July 31|work=The Baltimore Sun|date=May 26, 2016|url=http://www.baltimoresun.com/business/bs-bz-mars-closing-stores-20160525-story.html|access-date=May 29, 2016}} In July 2016, it was announced that Weis Markets entered into a purchase agreement with [[Ahold]] and [[Delhaize Group]] for 38 [[Food Lion]] locations in [[Maryland]], [[Delaware]], and [[Virginia]] as part of the divestiture of stores to gain clearance from the [[Federal Trade Commission]] for the impending Ahold/Delhaize merger.{{cite news|title=Ahold and Delhaize Group reach agreements with buyers to divest 86 U.S. stores, subject to FTC merger clearance|publisher=Food Lion|url=http://newsroom.foodlion.com/press-release/business-brand/delhaize-group-and-ahold-reach-agreements-buyers-divest-86-us-stores|access-date=July 13, 2016}} The company completed the acquisition and conversion of the stores in early November 2016. On March 9, 2017, Weis Markets opened a {{convert|65000|sqft|m2|0|adj=on}} store in [[Hampden Township, Pennsylvania]], that features a pub, ice cream parlor, expanded takeout food selection, a drive-thru pharmacy, and a beer cafe selling 900 varieties of beer and 500 varieties of wine.{{cite web|last=Gleiter|first=Sue|title=Here's a sneak peek of the new Weis Markets store opening in Cumberland County|publisher=PennLive.com|date=March 3, 2017|url=http://www.pennlive.com/food/index.ssf/2017/03/weis_markets_enola_1.html|access-date=March 17, 2017}} In late September 2019, Weis acquired two Thomas' Food Market stores, one in [[Dallas, Pennsylvania]] and another in [[Shavertown, Pennsylvania]], reopening the Dallas location under the Weis banner and closing the Shavertown location.{{Cite web|url=https://www.timesleader.com/news/757345/weis-acquires-thomas-food-market-stores-in-dallas-shavertown|title=Weis acquires Thomas' Food Market stores in Dallas, Shavertown|last=Leader|first=Times|date=2019-09-30|website=Times Leader|language=en-US|access-date=2020-02-11}} On July 19, 2018 Weis Markets opened a second store in [[Morris County, New Jersey|Morris County NJ]] in the [[Randolph, New Jersey|town of Randolph]] (where a former A&P used to operate before A&P's bankruptcy in 2015).{{Cite web|title=WEIS MARKETS OPENS NEW STORE IN RANDOLPH, NJ {{!}} Weis Markets|url=https://www.weismarkets.com/weis-markets-opens-new-store-randolph-nj|access-date=2020-06-18|website=www.weismarkets.com}} ===Legal case=== The Weis supermarket located in Park Hills Plaza along [[U.S. Route 220 in Pennsylvania|U.S. Route 220]] in [[Altoona, Pennsylvania]], was the subject of a key 1960s [[United States Supreme Court]] case concerning the "public forum doctrine." The Court held that a union picket in the supermarket parcel pickup area and parking lot was permissible because the "shopping center here is clearly the functional equivalent to the business district" of a city.Amalgamated Food Employees Union v. Logan Valley Plaza, Inc., 391 U.S. 308 (1968). At the time of the picketing, the Weis store was located in [[Logan Valley Mall]], the Park Hills Plaza was not built until the mid-1970s, at which time Weis moved across U.S. Route 220 to its current location. ===Shooting=== {{main|Eaton Township Weis Markets shooting}} In the early hours on the morning of June 8, 2017, employees at a Weis Markets [[supermarket]] in [[Eaton Township, Pennsylvania]], United States, were stocking and closing the store for the night. Shortly before 1:00 a.m., 24-year-old Randy Stair barricaded the exits of the store and proceeded to shoot and kill three of his co-workers before fatally shooting himself.{{Cite web|url=http://wnep.com/2017/06/08/victims-shooter-identified-in-weis-markets-murder-suicide/|title=Victims, Shooter Identified in Weis Markets Murder-Suicide|date=2017-06-08|website=WNEP.com|access-date=2017-06-21}} ==Banners== In addition to the Weis Markets banner, the company once operated supermarkets under the King's and Mr. Z's banners. Those two banners were centered primarily in the Lehigh Valley and the Poconos, respectively, and were acquired in 1993 (Mr.Z's) and 1994 (King's).{{Cite news|last=Shope|first=Dan|url=https://www.mcall.com/news/mc-xpm-1994-06-26-2970465-story.html|title=WEIS BUYS KING'S SIX MARKETS|date=June 26, 1994|work=The Morning Call|access-date=February 11, 2020}}{{Cite news | last=Zwiebach | first=Elliot | url=https://www.supermarketnews.com/archive/weis-construct-10-new-stores | title=WEIS TO CONSTRUCT 10 NEW STORES | work=Supermarket News | date=April 25, 1994}} Since their acquisitions, these stores have been remodeled or replaced. In 2009, they were rebranded to the Weis banner, as was its Cressler's store in Shippensburg. In 2011, it converted its three Scot's Lo-Cost stores, a warehouse store concept, located in Montoursville, Mill Hall, and Coal Township, to the Weis banner. At one time, the company operated a few stores as '''Big-Top Market''', but as of 2006, no more stores exist under this banner. Weis Markets owned a majority-stake in, and operated, a chain of pet supply warehouse stores called '''SuperPetz'''. The first SuperPetz store opened in 1991 in Dayton, Ohio. Weis Markets acquired an 80% stake in the chain in late 1993.{{cite news |last=Saxton |first=Lisa |date=1994-05-30 |title=Weis, SuperPetz Link Stirs Industry Interest |url=https://www.supermarketnews.com/archive/weis-superpetz-link-stirs-industry-interest |work=Supermarket News |access-date=2022-09-23}} Some stores included grooming services, dog training, and veterinary clinics. While their now-defunct website indicated they had 33 pet stores in eleven states in 2003, their footprint shrunk to only seven stores in June 2011, all of which were in Pennsylvania. None remain today. {{Cite web |url=http://www.superpetz.com/companyinfo.php |title=SuperPetz.com - Company Info |access-date=September 23, 2022 |archive-date=June 22, 2003 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20030622121442/http://www.superpetz.com/companyinfo.php |url-status=bot: unknown }} ==Private brand labels== [[File:Weis Markets store in Huntingdon Valley PA.jpeg|thumb|Weis Markets store in [[Huntingdon Valley, Pennsylvania]], formerly a [[Pathmark]]]] Weis Markets sells a variety of house brands under the following private brand labels: *Weis Quality (Advertised as equivalent to national brands) *Weis Organic (Organic Fruits and Vegetables) *Weis Signature (Premium) *Weis Quality Premium Meats (Deli Meat) *Paws Premium (Dog food) *TopCare (Health and Beauty Care Products) *Full Circle (Fair-Trade Certified food) *Weis 360 (Organic staples such as oatmeal and bread) *Weis Simply Great ==References== {{Reflist}} *DeKok, David.
